offence_severity: Minimum 6 months to maximum 2 years of rigorous imprisonment
number_of_offences: Multiple offences charged, but the number of offences finally upheld is not stated
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the appellant had compensated the complainant by repaying the entire amount of Rs.1.55 crore and an additional Rs.10 lacs towards interest for delayed payment.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses' credibility by noting that the transaction between the parties was purely civil in nature and did not attract criminal law.
post_offence_conduct: The appellant was in jail for more than 1 year before being released on bail and had also compensated the complainant and deposited an additional amount of Rs.10 lacs towards interest for delayed payment.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 2012; Trial judgment: 25.05.2015/29.05.2015; High Court decision: 29.11.2022; Supreme Court decision: 08.08.2023
legal_representation: Ashish Kumar Tiwari, Adv. for the Appellant; Birender Bikram, DAG, Samar Vijay Singh, Keshav Mittal, Ms. Sabarni Som, Fateh Singh, M. K. Dua, Shantanu Sagar, Anil Kumar, Gunjesh Ranjan, Advs. for the Respondents
investigation_status: FIR registered (FIR No.35 of 2014), charge sheet filed (21.07.2014), trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: conviction and sentence awarded; High Court: impugned order dated 29.11.2022; Supreme Court: appeal allowed, conviction and sentence set aside
prosecution_argument: The State argued that the complainant did not agree to compound the offence, and thus the courts cannot compel the complainant to give consent for compounding. The complainant's unwillingness to compound the case should not be ignored, and the criminal proceedings should continue.
defence_argument: The accused argued that he had fully compensated the complainant and that the criminal proceedings should be quashed as the complainant's unwillingness to compound the case was not a valid reason to continue the proceedings. The accused also emphasized that the transaction was civil in nature and did not attract criminal law.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that while the Negotiable Instruments Act makes offences compoundable, the consent of the complainant is still a necessary condition for compounding. The Court also emphasized that quashing a case is different from compounding and that the court has discretion to quash proceedings if the accused has fully compensated the complainant.
precedent_relied_upon: Damodar S. Prabhu v. Sayed Babalal H. [2010] 5 SCR 678 : (2010) 5 SCC 663; K.M Ibrahim v. K.P Mohammed & Anr. [2009] 15 SCR 1300 : (2010) 1 SCC 798; O.P Dholakia v. State of Haryana & Anr. (2000) 1 SCC 762; JIK Industries Limited & Ors. v. Amarlal V. Jamuni & Anr. [2012] 3 SCR 114 : (2012) 3 SCC 255; Meters and Instruments Private Ltd. And Another. v. Kanchan Mehta [2017] 10 SCR 66 : (2018) 1 SCC 560
judicial_mitigating_factors: The appellant had already been in jail for over a year, had fully compensated the complainant, and had deposited an additional amount of Rs.10 lacs towards interest for delayed payment.
other_sentence_order: The Supreme Court quashed all pending criminal appeals, set aside the conviction and sentence awarded by the trial court, and directed the trial court to hand over the Demand Drafts totalling Rs.30 lacs to the complainant.
